title: I want to play in the style of John Mayer
goal: Play the three sides of John Mayer: thumb-chord rhythm, the acoustic thumb-slap groove and blues-rooted lead phrasing.

phases.title: Blues Roots and the Lead Hand

steps.title: Where his blues comes from
steps.description:
[Before you start]
This roadmap is for an intermediate player. You need clean barre chords, a 12-bar blues in a shuffle feel, and the minor pentatonic somewhere on the neck.
You also need to play with your fingers. The whole acoustic phase is fingerstyle. There is no pick in it at all. If you have only ever used one, spend a week on plain thumb-and-finger picking before you get there.
Two early steps, pentatonic shapes and bending, are there to check and fix, not to teach. If yours are solid, use them to find what is not, then move on.
By the end you will play the three sides of Mayer's guitar: thumb-chord rhythm with embellishments, the thumb-slap acoustic groove, and blues lead in his phrasing. On your own rig, with a three-song set recorded.

[What it is]
A listening list and one drill.
Mayer got a Stevie Ray Vaughan cassette from a neighbour at 13. From there he worked backwards through Buddy Guy, B.B. King, Freddie King, Otis Rush and Hendrix, and later through the soul rhythm guitar of Curtis Mayfield and Steve Cropper.
The drill is the form all of that sits on. A 12-bar blues in A, with A7, D7 and E7 fretted with the thumb over the neck, played as a shuffle.

[Why it matters]
Everything in his electric playing comes from those players, and he took them one at a time.
If you copy only Mayer, you copy a copy. A copy is always thinner than the thing itself. Knowing where a lick came from is what lets you use it your own way instead of quoting it.
The 12-bar in A is where most of his electric playing lives. That makes it the first form to have under your hands.

[How to practice]
Make a playlist and listen to one track before each session: "Texas Flood" (Vaughan), "The Thrill Is Gone" (B.B. King), "Hide Away" (Freddie King), a live Buddy Guy cut, "Little Wing" and "Bold as Love" (Hendrix), "People Get Ready" (Curtis Mayfield). Then three of his own: "Who Did You Think I Was", "Gravity" and a live "Neon".
For each player, write down one thing you hear in them that you also hear in Mayer.
Then play the 12-bar in A at 80-100 BPM with a shuffle feel in Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords. Thumb on the sixth string, first finger free.
Watch the 2008 Berklee clinic when you have an hour. He plays and explains most of this roadmap in one evening.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a 12-bar shuffle in A at 90 BPM with thumb-fretted A7, D7 and E7, all the way through without stopping. For six of his influences you can name one recording and one thing he took from it.

lessons.title: John Mayer Teaching at Berklee College of Music (Full Berklee Clinic 2008)

steps.title: Pentatonic: box one and its neighbours
steps.description:
[What it is]
The A minor pentatonic box at the fifth fret, plus the shape below it (frets 2-5) and the shape above it (frets 7-10).
Mayer calls the border between two shapes the pentatonic equator. He teaches learning the shape below the one everybody knows, so a line can cross the border instead of bouncing around inside one box.

[Why it matters]
Your solos travel exactly as far as your shapes do.
A player who knows one box plays box-one licks, then has to jump to carry on. The jump is audible.
Mayer's lines move sideways instead. The Gravity solo walks up the second string through several shapes and never restarts.
What you are training here is not the shape itself, which you already have. It is the overlap between shapes.

[How to practice]
Check box one first: play it clean at 90 BPM.
Then learn the shape below it and the shape above it.
Then connect them in Improv — One String. One string is all you get, so every position change has to be a slide instead of a jump.
Take a three-note idea from box one and move it into both neighbouring shapes without stopping. Do it in A, then G, then E.
Finish over a slow blues backing track: find the same lick in three places on the neck.
steps.successCriteria: You can play A minor pentatonic in box one and both neighbouring shapes cleanly at 90 BPM. You can move a three-note lick between the shapes on slides, without a break, in A, G and E.

steps.title: Bend in tune
steps.description:
[What it is]
Bends that land exactly on the note you were aiming at. Whole step and half step, driven by rotating the wrist, with the fingers behind the bending finger helping to push.
Then two extras: the quarter-tone curl, which stops halfway between the minor and the major third, and the pre-bend, where you bend silently, pick, and let the note fall.

[Why it matters]
A bend that lands flat is the loudest mistake on the instrument. His never do.
His bends are slow and deliberate, taken from B.B. King. The note arrives at pitch and then sits there.
The quarter tone is the blues note that sits between happy and sad, and it is one of the most recognisable things in his playing.

[How to practice]
Bending — Match the Reference. Play the reference note, take a full half note to bend up to it, hold it, release slowly.
Whole steps first, on the second string. In G, bend the A at the tenth fret up to B. That is the move that opens Gravity.
Then half steps.
Then the quarter tone: over an A7 chord, curl the C on the second string up a quarter tone and listen for the blues. Then push it a full half step to C sharp and hear the difference.
Then pre-bends: bend to pitch before you pick, pick, release over two beats.
Record ten bends against a tuner and count how many land.
steps.successCriteria: Nine out of ten whole-step and half-step bends land in tune and hold there, with a slow even release. A quarter-tone curl over A7 sounds bluesy rather than flat. A pre-bend lands on pitch on the way down.

lessons.title: Bending and Vibrato (In the style of John Mayer)

steps.title: Slow, wide vibrato
steps.description:
[What it is]
An even vibrato from the wrist on a held note, with the pitch centre staying put.
Then vibrato on top of a bend without losing the target note.
Then the late start: let the note speak plainly for a beat, and only then begin to move it.

[Why it matters]
Vibrato is what keeps a long note alive instead of letting it just fade.
The Gravity solo is mostly long notes with vibrato and bends, and that vibrato is slow, wide and even. It is not the fast nervous shake most players fall into.
Until you can choose its speed and width on purpose, every phrase in this roadmap lands on a note that is already wobbling.

[How to practice]
Vibrato — Speed & Width, on held notes and on bent notes, choosing the width and the speed rather than letting them happen.
Then Vibrato — Hold a Whole Bar with its backing track, switching the vibrato on and off on exact beats.
Then the late start: play a G on the second string, eighth fret, straight for one beat, then a slow wide vibrato for three.
On a bend, oscillate below the target and back up to it, so the top of the vibrato is the note you bent to.
Record that held G and play it back to back with the first note of the Gravity solo.
steps.successCriteria: You can hold a note with an even vibrato at two speeds and two widths on request, with the pitch centre stable. Vibrato at the top of a whole-step bend stays in tune. A four-beat note with a delayed start sounds like the first note of the Gravity solo.

lessons.title: Develop Your Bending Vibrato With This Simple Exercise
Make YOUR Vibrato sound awesome (Guitar Lesson)

steps.title: Slides and legato
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing along the neck instead of across it. Slides into notes and between positions, plus hammer-ons and pull-offs on one string.
The line follows a single string up the neck rather than sitting inside a box.

[Why it matters]
Mayer uses slides and hammer-ons for three jobs at once: as passing notes, as the way he changes position, and as a way to start a phrase without attacking it.
The Gravity solo hammers, pulls off and slides along the second string.
Slurred notes have to be as loud as picked ones. If they are not, the line goes lumpy the moment you stop picking.

[How to practice]
Legato — Scale Run, slowly, until hammer-ons and pull-offs are as loud as picked notes. That evenness is the whole point, and it will not survive being played fast if you skip it now.
Then take a slow blues in G and solo on the second string alone. Every position change is a slide. Put a rest between phrases.
Do the same on the third string, then in A minor pentatonic on the first.
Learn three licks from the Darryl Syms legato lesson and play them along one string in two keys.
steps.successCriteria: Over a backing track in G you can improvise for two minutes on the second string alone, with a slide for every position change and slurred notes as loud as picked ones. You can play the slides in the Gravity intro line in time with the record.

lessons.title: The John Mayer Legato Trick | [ HOW TO + LICKS ]

steps.title: Rakes and double stops
steps.description:
[What it is]
A rake is a drag of the pick across muted strings into one fretted note, so the note arrives with a scrape in front of it. You hear it all over "Who Did You Think I Was".
A double stop is two notes played together on neighbouring strings, usually a fourth apart, with every other string silent. That is the "Slow Dancing" intro riff.

[Why it matters]
This is the grit that keeps his electric playing from sounding polite.
The rake is the Stevie Ray Vaughan attack. The double stop is the other half: two notes carry more weight than one.
Both only work if everything around them is silent, so this is a muting step as much as a picking step.

[How to practice]
Muting — One Note at a Time. Palm resting on the lower strings, first finger laid flat across the higher ones, one note allowed to ring.
Then the rake. With the same muting, drag the pick across three strings into the eighth fret of the first string, so only that note has any pitch. Slowly at first, then at a 90 BPM shuffle, on every string.
Then double stops. Fourths on the first and second strings, then on the second and third, inside box one, with the side of the thumb killing the rest.
Finish with the Slow Dancing intro figure. You will meet it again as a whole song later.
steps.successCriteria: A rake gives you one clear note with a scrape in front of it and no ringing neighbours, on any string, at a 90 BPM shuffle. Double stops in fourths ring evenly with everything else silent. You can play a pentatonic double-stop lick that starts with a rake.

lessons.title: 10 Tasteful John Mayer Licks (John Mayer Guitar Lesson)

steps.title: Thumb over the neck
steps.description:
[What it is]
An E-shape barre chord where the thumb frets the sixth string and mutes the fifth. The first finger is then free, and so are the others.
The same grip gives two of his signature chords: Dmaj7 with the thumb on the root (Gravity) and Badd11 with the thumb on B and the first string open (Slow Dancing in a Burning Room).

[Why it matters]
This one grip is what makes the rest of his rhythm playing possible.
A barre chord uses all four fingers to hold a sound. A thumb chord uses two or three and leaves the little finger free to add notes.
The embellishments in Slow Dancing cannot be played from a normal barre. There are no spare fingers.
Every step in this phase, and the whole acoustic phase, sits on this grip.

[How to practice]
Bring the neck up and let the wrist drop, so the thumb can reach over.
Start with F at the first fret. Thumb on F, fifth string muted by the side of the thumb, fingers on the fourth, third and second strings. Move the same shape to G, A and B flat.
Then Dmaj7: thumb on the tenth fret of the sixth string, fingers on the eleventh fret of the fourth and third strings and the tenth of the second, first string muted.
Then Badd11: thumb on the seventh fret, ninth fret of the fourth string, eighth of the third, seventh of the second, first string open.
Loop F, G, A, B flat in Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords at 60-80 BPM. Pick each chord string by string to check it before you strum it.
steps.successCriteria: You can hold thumb-fretted F, G, A and B flat with every intended string clean and the fifth string silent, and change between them in quarter notes at 80 BPM. Dmaj7 and Badd11 both ring cleanly.

lessons.title: Thumb Barre Chords - How and Why - Jimi Hendrix, John Frusciante, John Mayer Rhythm Guitar Tutorial
Play in the Style of Hendrix and John Mayer with THUMB-Over Chords
Thumb Over the Neck Chords, Frethand Muting, and Choosing the Right Guitar

steps.title: Decorate chords with the little finger
steps.description:
[What it is]
The thumb holds the bass. The little finger and ring finger hammer on and pull off the fourth, the sixth and the ninth on the strings above it.
One held chord turns into a moving figure. That is "Little Wing", "Bold as Love", the verse of Slow Dancing and the intro of Waiting on the World to Change.

[Why it matters]
This is the core of his rhythm playing.
It is why one guitar under his ballads sounds like a band, and why his parts keep moving even when the chord does not change.

[How to practice]
Take a thumb-fretted G at the third fret.
Hammer the fourth with the little finger and pull off again: C, fifth fret of the third string.
Then the sixth: E, fifth fret of the second string.
Then the ninth: A, second fret of the third string.
Use Chords — Degree Hunt (Triads) until you can find the 4, the 6 and the 9 of any chord without thinking.
Then loop G, C and D at 70 BPM with one decoration per chord, on beats 2 and 4, in a lazy sixteenth feel. The thumb never lifts off the bass.
Then learn the Slow Dancing verse figure from the Marty Music and Dan Guitar lessons.
steps.successCriteria: Over a G, C, D loop at 70 BPM you can add a sus4, 6 or 9 to every chord with hammer-ons and pull-offs while the thumb holds the bass, name the note you are adding, and keep the groove going. You can play the Slow Dancing verse figure at tempo.

lessons.title: Embellishing Guitar Chords Like Hendrix and Mayer

steps.title: Move the bass under the chord
steps.description:
[What it is]
Chords with the third in the bass instead of the root, fretted with the thumb. D/F sharp with the thumb on the second fret is the one to start with.
Then bass notes that walk by step under the chords: D, D/F sharp, G, A. Or G, G/B, C.
Also Emaj9 with the open sixth string, the chord under "No Such Thing".

[Why it matters]
Chords that jump from root to root sound like a chart being read out.
A bass that walks by step under the same chords sounds like a bass player and a keyboard working together. That is the D/F sharp in Waiting on the World to Change.
Because the thumb is holding the bass note, the fingers stay free for the hammer-ons from the last step.

[How to practice]
Chords — Least Finger Motion with D, D/F sharp, G, A. Keep the notes that repeat, move only the bass, and move it by step.
Then the Waiting on the World to Change verse and chorus from the Andy Guitar and Jorge Aguilera lessons: D, Bm, G, A, with the inversion and the hammer-ons the way he plays them, thumb on the F sharp.
Then G, G/B, C, D the same way.
Finish with Emaj9: open sixth string, root at the twelfth fret. Let it ring.
steps.successCriteria: You can play D, D/F sharp, G, A and G, G/B, C, D with the bass moving by step under your thumb and no gap between chords at 80 BPM. You can play the Waiting on the World to Change verse and chorus in time with the record.

lessons.title: How to Play "Waiting on the World to Change" on Guitar - John Mayer Lesson

[HOW TO] Play Chords Like Hendrix and Mayer

steps.title: Fills from the chord you are holding
steps.description:
[What it is]
Play the chord. Then play single notes from the pentatonic that sits in the same place as that chord shape. Then come back to the chord.
The fill belongs to the chord because it comes out of the chord's own shape. You hear it in "Another Kind of Green", Slow Dancing and "Bold as Love".

[Why it matters]
This is the bridge between his rhythm playing and his lead playing, and the reason his fills never sound like a solo interrupting the song.
Learn it once and you stop hunting for a scale every time a gap opens up.

[How to practice]
Thumb-fretted G at the third fret, with the G major pentatonic shape that surrounds it. Chord on beat 1, fill on beats 3 and 4, chord again.
Then C at the eighth fret with C major pentatonic. Then D at the tenth.
Then Improv — Chord Tones over a G, C, D loop, aiming each fill at a note of the chord you are about to land on.
Then try it minor: thumb-fretted Am at the fifth fret with A minor pentatonic box one.
Keep the thumb down during the fill so the bass never disappears.
steps.successCriteria: Over G, C, D thumb chords at 80 BPM you can alternate a bar of chord with a bar of fill drawn from that chord's own position, changing shape on every chord, for two minutes, with every fill landing on a chord tone on the next downbeat.

lessons.title: Tasty Licks using your Thumb on the guitar neck (Hendrix, John Mayer Technique)

steps.title: Sixths
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two notes a sixth apart, moved through the scale as a pair. They sit on the third and first strings, or on the fourth and second, with the string in between muted.
This is the soul vocabulary he uses in the "Your Body Is a Wonderland" solo, in the live acoustic Gravity intro, and in most of his fills.

[Why it matters]
Sixths are the sweetest sound in his playing, and they come from sixties soul rather than from blues. Curtis Mayfield and Steve Cropper are where he got them.
Two notes a sixth apart make one guitar sound like a horn section, which is exactly what you want under a vocal.

[How to practice]
Note Hunt — Intervals set to major and minor sixths, until you find one instantly from any note.
Then play the G major scale in sixths on the third and first strings, from the third fret up and back, at 60 BPM. Use the pick and middle finger, or fingers alone. The string in between stays silent.
Do the same on the fourth and second strings.
Then use sixths as fills over G, C, D, and over the Gravity verse.
Finish by learning the sixths in the Your Body Is a Wonderland solo from a transcription.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the G major scale in sixths on two string pairs, up and down the neck at 80 BPM, with the middle string silent. You can drop sixths into a I-IV-V in G and in D, and play the sixths in the Your Body Is a Wonderland solo at tempo.

lessons.title: Mastering John Mayer's Double Stop Patterns

steps.title: Sixteenth-note comping
steps.description:
[What it is]
The picking hand never stops moving in sixteenths. The fretting hand decides which of those strokes ring.
Some are short chord stabs. Most are muted scratches with no pitch. The phrase ends with a double-stop fill.
This is the part under Waiting on the World to Change and "Heart of Life", played clean on a Strat.

[Why it matters]
Mayer sets the standard for this job himself: "If I'm doing my job right, you shouldn't have to pay attention to what I'm playing."
A part that grooves without drawing attention is the hardest thing in this roadmap to fake.
It also puts the last four steps together. Thumb chords, partial shapes, sixths and muting are each easy on their own and hard at the same time.

[How to practice]
Strumming — Funk 16ths at 70-90 BPM, until the hand keeps moving on its own.
Then the same motion over thumb-chord voicings: Em7, G6, D, A. Two stabs per bar ring, everything else is a scratch.
Then add a sixths fill on the last beat of every second bar.
Record it over a drum loop at 88 BPM. Listen back and ask yourself what you noticed first, the groove or the guitar. It should be the groove.
steps.successCriteria: Over a drum loop at 85-95 BPM you can comp a D major progression (D, Bm, G, A, with Em7 and G6) for three minutes with the hand moving constantly in sixteenths, only the chosen stabs ringing, and the scratches with no pitch in them.

lessons.title: Comping Rhythms - 10 Examples You Need To Know
Rhythm Guitar Lesson Using String Muting Techniques

steps.title: Thumb and index only
steps.description:
[What it is]
His acoustic right hand uses two things: the thumb, playing bass on beats 1 and 3 like a kick drum, and the index finger, which does everything else.
The index either pinches a string together with the thumb, or flicks across the top three strings.
Whole chords are sometimes plucked with thumb and three fingers at once and stopped immediately. There is no pick anywhere in this phase.

[Why it matters]
The hand is simpler than it sounds. Almost everything you will play in this phase is thumb, index, or both at the same time.
The slap in the next step only works over a thumb bass that never wavers. That is why the bass is built first and on its own.

[How to practice]
Fingerstyle — Descending Arpeggios, to get the thumb and fingers working apart from each other over a moving bass.
Then hold Dsus2, the shape under "Stop This Train" and "Who Says". Thumb on the fourth string on beats 1 and 3. Index pinches the first string together with the thumb on beat 1, then flicks the top three strings on the "and" of 2.
Loop that at 70 BPM, then move the same pattern through G, Em and C.
Finish with the piano pluck: grab the whole chord with thumb and three fingers, stop it dead, repeat on every beat.
steps.successCriteria: You can keep a thumb bass on beats 1 and 3 through a Dsus2, G, Em, C loop at 80 BPM, with the index pinching on 1 and flicking the top strings on the "and" of 2, for two minutes with the bass at an even volume.

lessons.title: The John Mayer Fingerstyle Technique in 6 Steps
The John Mayer Thumb & Flick Technique

steps.title: The thumb slap
steps.description:
[What it is]
The side of the thumb hitting the low strings on beats 2 and 4, driven by a quick turn of the wrist, like turning a key.
The guitar ends up carrying its own snare drum.

[Why it matters]
The slap is the snare in Neon, Stop This Train, Who Says and Heart of Life. The whole acoustic side runs on it.
Like a snare, it has to sound identical every single time. One weak slap in sixteen bars is heard as a mistake, not as a variation.
That is why you drill it on its own before any song is attached to it.

[How to practice]
Dry first. Slaps only, on 2 and 4, with a metronome at 60-90 BPM, for a full minute. Record it and listen for the weak one.
Then add the thumb bass on 1 and 3, so the bar reads kick, snare, kick, snare.
Then Hybrid Picking — Bass + Chords, to get the bass and the chord working together, and put the slap in between.
Finish by holding a Dsus2 and running kick, slap, kick, slap for two minutes without dropping one.
steps.successCriteria: At 80 BPM your slaps on 2 and 4 are even in volume and timing across 16 bars of a recording. You can alternate thumb bass on 1 and 3 with slaps on 2 and 4 over a held Dsus2 for two minutes without missing one.

lessons.title: Play Like: John Mayer | Slapping thumb technique
John Mayer Style: Thumb Slap Percussive Rhythm Technique

steps.title: The slap-flick pattern
steps.description:
[What it is]
The six-part pattern that runs under Stop This Train and Who Says:
1. thumb and index pinch on beat 1
2. slap with an index flick across the top three strings on beat 2
3. index plucks the first string
4. thumb bass on beat 3
5. another pluck, this time on the third string
6. slap and flick again on beat 4
Played over Dsus2, G, E and A, with the thumb over the neck where the song needs it.

[Why it matters]
This is the real pattern behind those songs, not an approximation of it.
Once it runs on its own, the songs are just chord changes placed on top. The same pattern with different accents becomes the engine of Neon in the next step.
It is also the first place where the thumb-over left hand and the slap-and-flick right hand have to work at the same time.

[How to practice]
Build it one layer at a time, and do not add a layer until the one below it runs without thought.
Pinch only. Then add the slap-flick on 2. Then the pluck. Then the bass on 3. Then the second pluck. Then the slap-flick on 4.
Stay at 60 BPM through all of that. Then 80. Then song tempo.
Then learn the Stop This Train verse and chorus from the JustinGuitar Songs lesson, with the capo where the original has it, and play along with the record.
Record one minute and check two things: that the slaps are even, and that no bass note is missing.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the six-part pattern through Dsus2, G, E and A at 90 BPM for three minutes, with even slaps and no dropped bass notes. You can play the verse and chorus of Stop This Train with the record without stopping.

lessons.title: How to play Stop This Train by John Mayer on the guitar [Part 1]
Stop This Train by John Mayer Guitar Lesson
Stop This Train Guitar Tutorial John Mayer Guitar Lesson |Chords + Fingerpicking|

steps.title: Neon
steps.description:
[What it is]
The thumb-over chord shapes in C that Neon is built from, and the descending pattern they move through.
The dead notes that keep the groove ticking between them.
And, in the live version, a triplet played with the thumb alone: it slaps the muted sixth string, pushes through to pop it, then pops the fifth string.

[Why it matters]
Neon is how guitarists recognise Mayer, and it tests the last three steps at the same time.
That thumb triplet genuinely does not turn up in anyone else's playing.
Nothing here is new theory. It is the mechanics you already have, at full speed.

[How to practice]
Left hand first, with no rhythm at all. The thumb-over shapes and the descending pattern, slowly, until the changes are clean.
Then the right hand. Hybrid Picking — Chicken Pickin' for the snap of a popped string. Then the slap-pop-pop triplet from the Zartimus lesson, on muted strings, with a click at 60 BPM.
Then put them together two bars at a time, using the chasechocolate right-hand tutorial. Studio version before the live one.
Play with the record at half speed before you try it at full speed.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the Neon studio intro and verse pattern with the record at full speed for 32 bars without stopping, with the dead notes and slaps in place. You can play the slap-pop-pop triplet cleanly at 100 BPM on muted strings.

lessons.title: Neon John Mayer Guitar Tutorial (right hand and rhythm)
Neon by John Mayer (Live Version) Guitar Lesson
John Mayer Muted slap pop triplet technique with TAB

steps.title: Major pentatonic, short phrases
steps.description:
[What it is]
G major pentatonic over a held G or a I-IV loop, played as short ideas of two to four notes.
Each idea ends on a note of the chord. Then there is silence before the next one.
This is not a scale run in either direction.

[Why it matters]
Most of his pop leads are major pentatonic rather than minor. The Gravity solo is G major pentatonic from beginning to end.
The scale is the easy part. The hard part is stopping.
A short idea that resolves and then leaves a gap sounds composed. The same notes played without stopping sound like practice.

[How to practice]
Improv — One Chord over G. Use the G major pentatonic around the E-shape chord at the third fret, and the one around the C-shape at the eighth.
Play a four-bar phrase, then rest for four bars, then play again.
Sing each idea before you play it, and end it on B or D.
Then move to the Gravity verse loop, G to C6 in 6/8, and keep the same two rules: end on a chord tone, then stop.
steps.successCriteria: Over a G to C loop in 6/8 at 60 BPM you can improvise for three minutes with phrases that each end on a chord tone and are each followed by at least a bar of silence. You can sing back any phrase you have just played.

lessons.title: How to use the Major Pentatonic in a Blues (and sound good)
Blues Guitar Lesson (Phrasing) - How To Stop Playing The Pentatonic Scale Up And Down

steps.title: Mix major and minor pentatonic
steps.description:
[What it is]
Moving between the major and the minor pentatonic of the same root inside one phrase.
The minor third slides up to the major third. Major sits well over the I chord, minor over the IV and V, and the quarter tone in between belongs to both.
In A the two scales sit three frets apart and overlap. That overlap is what Mayer calls the equator.

[Why it matters]
This mixture is the sound of his blues.
Over a dominant chord both thirds are available at once, so you can move between them inside a single phrase and nothing sounds wrong.
The overlap is also why a B.B. King box seems to work over everything: it is made of notes both scales share.

[How to practice]
In A: minor box one at the fifth fret, major box at the second. Same shape, three frets down.
Over a 12-bar in A at 90 BPM, try it by chord. Major pentatonic over the I. Minor over the IV. Mixed over the V.
Then one line per chorus that slides the minor third up to the major third inside the phrase.
Use the Pentatonic Best Of play-alongs to do the same thing over real tracks.
Then add the small colours that live in the same place: a grace-note hammer from the minor third to the major third, a slide from the flat seventh into the root, and the quarter-tone curl from the bending step. Each one has to land on a chord tone within a beat, or it sounds like a wrong note instead of a colour.
steps.successCriteria: Over a 12-bar blues in A at a 90 BPM shuffle you can play a chorus with major pentatonic on the I, minor on the IV, and lines that move from the minor third to the major third inside one phrase, with nothing sounding wrong. You can say which notes changed.

lessons.title: Mixing Major & Minor Pentatonics In Blues - How, Why and What To Practice! Guitar Lesson Tutorial
Blend the major and minor pentatonic scales in 1 position - Guitar Lesson - ML074
How JOHN MAYER MIXES Major&minor PENTATONIC in BLUES! Part 1

steps.title: Aim at the chord tones
steps.description:
[What it is]
Pointing every phrase at a note of the chord you are about to land on. Usually the third: B over G, E over C.
That means hearing the change coming before it arrives.
Triad shapes, not scale shapes, are the map for this.

[Why it matters]
Target notes are why his simple lines sound composed.
A phrase that lands on the third of the new chord sounds intended. The same notes played straight through the change sound like an accident.
Gravity's chorus borrows chords from G minor, and his solo follows every one of them.

[How to practice]
Improv — Chord Tones over G to C in 6/8 first. Land the third on the downbeat of every change.
Then do the same over the Gravity chorus progression at 60 BPM, using triad shapes to see where the third of each chord is.
Chords — Degree Hunt (Changes) to get faster at finding them.
Then the real test: sing the target note during the bar before it arrives. If you can sing it, you can aim at it.
steps.successCriteria: Over the Gravity chorus progression at 60 BPM in 6/8 you land the third of every chord on the downbeat of the change, four cycles in a row. Over a I-IV-V in D you can aim at thirds or sixths on request.

lessons.title: Triads are the SECRET to good melody. Guitar Lesson - MicroLesson ML103

steps.title: Leave space
steps.description:
[What it is]
Silence used as part of the line, short stopped notes, and phrases placed a little behind the beat on purpose while your own pulse stays exactly on it.
The laid-back phrase works because it is rare.

[Why it matters]
Silence is the loudest thing in his playing, and it is a decision, not a gap while you think of the next note.
Playing a hair behind the beat is the other half. Used now and then it sounds relaxed. Used constantly it just sounds late.
Mayer compares his own job to lifting a couch with one finger: the effort should not show.

[How to practice]
Phrasing — Two Notes Per Bar over a slow 6/8 backing in G for three minutes. Then over a shuffle in A.
Then record the same eight-bar phrase twice: once right on the beat, once laid back by a hair. Listen back and decide which one sounds like him.
From here on, two rules for every solo you play: at least half the time is silence, and no more than one laid-back phrase every twelve bars.
steps.successCriteria: In a two-minute recorded improvisation, at least half the time is silence and the phrases are two to five notes long. One phrase per twelve bars is laid back and a listener hears it as deliberate. The pulse never wobbles.

lessons.title: Playing Behind The Beat - "The Art of Laying Back" | Guitar Lesson

steps.title: Call and response
steps.description:
[What it is]
Phrases in pairs: a question, then an answer.
Then one idea of three notes carried through a whole chorus. You repeat it, move it to the IV chord, change its rhythm, and end it differently each time.
The Gravity solo repeats its opening idea rather than replacing it.

[Why it matters]
Mayer says he cannot solo for long before he repeats himself. That is the design, not a limit.
An idea that comes back slightly changed is how a listener remembers a solo. A brand new run every four bars is how they forget it.
B.B. King's solos are conversations, and Mayer's answer his own vocal lines.

[How to practice]
Phrasing — Call & Response over a 12-bar in A. Every four bars is one call and one answer.
Then the motif work: pick one three-note idea and stay on it for twelve bars. Variations only, no new material. This will feel too restrictive, which is the point.
Then transcribe the first eight bars of the Gravity solo and mark every idea that comes back.
steps.successCriteria: Over a 12-bar blues you can play three choruses where every four bars is a call and an answer, and one chorus built from a single three-note idea with at least four variations that a listener still hears as the same idea.

lessons.title: Once I Learned This Call & Response My Blues Phrasing Changed Forever!
Call and Response Phrasing - Guitar Soloing School Lesson #4

steps.title: Sing what you play
steps.description:
[What it is]
Singing a line before you play it, and again while you play it.
Taking phrases from singers rather than from other guitarists: playing his vocal melodies on the guitar, with a slide or a bend wherever the voice slides.

[Why it matters]
Singing removes the delay between hearing an idea and playing it. That delay is what makes lines come out as shapes instead of sentences.
His advice to guitarists is to listen to singers. His solos copy his own vocal phrasing: phrases the length of one breath, and bends where a voice would slide up to a note.

[How to practice]
Sing What You Play, every session.
Then sing the vocal melody of Slow Dancing in a Burning Room. Then play it on the second and third strings, sliding or bending wherever the voice does.
Learn five licks from the Pickup Music lesson, singing each one before you play it.
Finish by recording a 24-bar solo where you sing every phrase out loud as you play it.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the vocal melody of Slow Dancing in a Burning Room or Daughters on guitar, with slides and bends matching the voice. In a recorded 24-bar solo where you sing along, the guitar matches the sung pitch on at least nine notes out of ten.

lessons.title: John Mayer Guitar Lesson on Instagram Live (May 7th 2020)
10 Tasteful John Mayer Licks (John Mayer Guitar Lesson)

steps.title: Hybrid picking
steps.description:
[What it is]
Pick and fingers at the same time. The pick handles the low string, the middle and ring fingers take the higher ones.
That gives you wide jumps between strings, thumb chords played as arpeggios, and sixths plucked as a pair.

[Why it matters]
This is how he moves from a strummed chord to a plucked fill inside one bar without putting the pick down.
It also reaches intervals no single pick stroke can, which is why some of his electric figures sound more like a piano part than a guitar one.

[How to practice]
Hybrid Picking — Wide Intervals for the mechanics.
Then arpeggiate thumb-fretted G, C and D at 80 BPM, with the pick on the sixth string and the fingers on the top three.
Then play the sixths from phase two with pick and middle finger instead of two fingers.
Then the real use: inside a strummed bar, switch to a plucked fill on beat 4 and back to strumming on beat 1, with no hesitation in between.
steps.successCriteria: At 90 BPM you can play wide string-skipping lines and arpeggiated thumb chords with pick and fingers, with picked and plucked notes at the same volume. You can switch from a strummed chord to a hybrid-picked fill inside one bar without hesitating.

lessons.title: Hybrid Picking Lesson For Guitar- What It Is And How To Do It
The 7 Best Hybrid Picking Exercises for Guitar

steps.title: Tone is in your hands
steps.description:
[What it is]
The part of your tone that has nothing to do with gear.
Near the bridge it is bright. Over the neck it is round. The edge of the pick sounds different from its face. Fingers sound different again.
The same lick, in four colours.

[Why it matters]
Almost all of his sound is touch on a clean amp. That is why this comes before any talk of gear, otherwise the rig step turns into shopping.
Where the pick hits the string, at what angle, and whether you use one at all, changes the tone more than any knob on the amp.
A clean sound with nothing added is also the fastest way to find the note that is not right yet. There is nothing to hide behind.

[How to practice]
Tone — Pick Position & Angle.
Then play one Mayer lick four ways: near the bridge, over the neck pickup, with the edge of the pick, and with thumb and index instead of a pick. Record all four back to back and say out loud what changed in each.
Then the honesty test. Clean Tone — Slow Melody, and after it the Gravity intro line on a clean sound with no reverb and no delay, recorded.
Listen to that recording three times. Once for the bends. Once for the vibrato. Once for the dynamics. Fix one thing per take.
steps.successCriteria: You can get three clearly different tones out of one lick by pick position and angle, and a fourth with your fingers, on request. A clean recording of the Gravity intro line has every bend in tune, even vibrato, no unwanted noise, and dynamics that rise into the last phrase.

lessons.title: Blueprints: John Mayer's Tonal Foundation
Guitar Dynamics Practice: Control Your Tone with This Simple Exercise

steps.title: Loud and soft
steps.description:
[What it is]
Three volume levels, produced by the hand alone.
A swell inside one phrase. A solo that starts quiet and peaks late. A comp that stays under the singer.

[Why it matters]
Mayer: "If I'm doing my job right, you shouldn't have to pay attention to what I'm playing."
His solos are shaped by volume far more than by the number of notes in them.
Three clearly different levels, made by the hand and not by a pedal, are what separate his version of a lick from a copy of it.

[How to practice]
Dynamics — Soft to Loud, to control how deep the pick goes.
Then play a 12-bar solo that starts as quietly as the chord will still ring, peaks in bar nine, and comes back down by the end.
Then comp along to a Mayer song at a volume where the vocal on the record always wins. If you can hear yourself over the singer, you are too loud.
steps.successCriteria: A recorded 12-bar solo rises in volume to bar nine and falls to the end, with the tempo unchanged. You can comp a Mayer song under its vocal at a level where the voice stays on top the whole way through.

lessons.title: How To Control The Dynamics In Your Guitar Playing
Picking control & Keep in Time with Metronome / TFGL#2

steps.title: The rig
steps.description:
[What it is]
A Strat-style guitar with single coils, on the neck or middle pickup.
A loud clean amp set right at the edge of breaking up.
A Tube Screamer or Blues Driver type pedal used as a light boost, not as distortion.
A little reverb or delay.
And how to get close to all of that on whatever amp or plugin you actually own.

[Why it matters]
The Continuum and Trio tones are this chain plus the touch from the last two steps. The amp reacts to how hard you play, which is why dynamics came first.
Matching a tone by ear also teaches you to hear what changed, so the settings move with you to other rigs instead of being one set of numbers.

[How to practice]
Tone — Match the Reference.
Set the clean amp so that a hard strum just breaks up. Set the overdrive with the drive low and the level high, so it pushes the amp rather than distorting on its own.
Neck pickup for the Gravity sound. Middle, or bridge and middle, for Slow Dancing.
Compare against the records and change one control at a time.
Save three settings: clean comping, edge-of-breakup lead, boosted lead. Write each one down in words rather than numbers, so it still makes sense on someone else's amp.
steps.successCriteria: You have three saved settings on your own rig: clean comping, edge-of-breakup lead and boosted lead. Recordings of them sit next to the Gravity and Slow Dancing references without sounding harsh, and you can describe each one in words for a different rig.

lessons.title: How to Dial in John Mayer Guitar Tones with Tim Marco
How To Sound Like John Mayer with Effects Pedals | Reverb Potent Pairings
I simplified John Mayer's pedalboard to its 7 key effects

steps.title: Learn a part by ear
steps.description:
[What it is]
Working out a piece of his playing from the recording alone, with no tab open.
Finding the key. Hearing where the chords change. Deciding whether a chord is major, minor or dominant. Copying a short lick note for note, by singing it back first.

[Why it matters]
Tabs of his parts are often wrong, and they are wrong in the same two places every time: the voicing under the thumb, and the exact fret a bend starts from.
More importantly, every step before this one taught you what to listen for. You now have a reason to listen instead of to read.
This is also the one skill here that keeps growing after the roadmap ends.

[How to practice]
Play by Ear — Easy every session, to sharpen pitch matching.
Then pick something short: an intro figure, a two-bar fill, or the first phrase of a solo.
Hum the note the phrase settles on and find it on the low E string. That gives you the key.
Count bars out loud through the section and mark where every chord changes.
For each chord, try the likely candidates in that key and keep the one that matches the bass.
Then sing the lick, play it, and compare both against the record.
One short piece per week is enough.
steps.successCriteria: You can take a two-bar figure from a Mayer song you have never seen a tab for, find its key, write down its chords and play it with the record, in under thirty minutes. You can sing the phrase back before you play it.

lessons.title: How to Identify Chord Progressions by Ear - Music Theory for Guitarists Unit 2 Lesson 3
How To Figure Out The KEY Of A Song by EAR On Guitar | GUITAR EAR TRAINING

steps.title: Gravity
steps.description:
[What it is]
The whole song.
Verses of G to C6 in 6/8. A chorus that borrows chords from G minor: Am7, D7, Gm/B flat, E flat maj7, D7. The thumb-fretted Dmaj7.
Both solos in G major pentatonic, sitting around the G on the second string at the eighth fret, with the A-to-B bend, slides along the string, and long notes with vibrato.

[Why it matters]
Gravity contains this entire roadmap. B.B. King bends and vibrato. Horizontal legato. Target notes over borrowed chords. A thumb-fretted voicing. Dynamics from a whisper to full.
Every skill you have practised has an audible job inside one song, which is why it comes first here.

[How to practice]
Rhythm first: the verse in 6/8 with the Dmaj7 voicing, then the chorus arpeggiated in even eighth notes.
Then the intro line from the JustinGuitar solo lesson.
Then the main solo from the Acoustic Experience breakdown, at half speed with the tab.
Play the whole thing with the record.
Then improvise your own sixteen bars over the verse loop, using the same language.
steps.successCriteria: You can play Gravity with the record from start to finish, rhythm and both solos, in time and with every bend in tune. You can improvise sixteen bars over the verse loop using major pentatonic, target thirds, space and one laid-back phrase.

lessons.title: Gravity by John Mayer * Solos * Guitar Lesson
John Mayer Gravity Lead Guitar + Chords Lesson/Tutorial
John Mayer Gravity Guitar Tutorial | Solo & Intro Breakdown (Slow + Tabs)

steps.title: Slow Dancing in a Burning Room
steps.description:
[What it is]
The song in C sharp minor and E.
Thumb chords through the verse, pre-chorus and chorus, decorated the way phase two taught. The Badd11 with the first string open. The double-stop intro riff.
Then a solo of short licks that ends in a run of fast double-stop slides.

[Why it matters]
This is the clearest recording of the Hendrix side of Mayer, and the exam for phases one and two together.
The decorations cannot be played from a normal barre, so the thumb grip is not optional here.
The double-stop slides at the end of the solo will show you exactly how clean your muting is.

[How to practice]
Verse and chorus with thumb chords from the Marty Music lesson, then the less obvious voicings from the Sound Guitar Lessons version.
The intro riff as double stops, with the muting from phase one.
The solo from the GuitarZero2Hero lesson at half speed with the tab. Leave the double-stop slides until last.
Play it with the record, then record yourself playing it without stopping.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the verse, pre-chorus and chorus with thumb chords and decorations in time with the record, the intro riff cleanly, and the solo at tempo including the double-stop slides, all in one recording without stopping.

lessons.title: John Mayer Slow Dancing in a Burning Room Guitar Lesson + Tutorial
Slow Dancing in a Burning Room Chords - Unique John Mayer Guitar Lesson
Slow Dancing In A Burning Room Guitar Tutorial John Mayer Lesson |Electric Lesson + Solo + TAB|

steps.title: Who Did You Think I Was
steps.description:
[What it is]
The song that defines the John Mayer Trio, the 2005 band with Pino Palladino on bass and Steve Jordan on drums.
A riff built around an A7 chord. Minor pentatonic phrases that start with a rake. A chorus of F sharp minor and G played in a very Hendrix way.

[Why it matters]
Mayer formed the Trio to play what he called "power-rockin', electric-guitar, in-your-face blues". This is where the Vaughan and Hendrix material from phase one becomes his own.
A dominant chord with minor pentatonic over it is the Trio sound in one sentence.
The rhythm part also has to leave room for a bass player and a drummer, which is what the next phase is about.

[How to practice]
The riff first, from the Marty Music or Jon MacLennan lesson, with the rakes into the A.
Then the chorus. Then the full song with the record.
Finish by improvising 24 bars over an A7 vamp, mixing A minor pentatonic with the C sharp that belongs to the chord.
steps.successCriteria: You can play Who Did You Think I Was from start to finish with the record, and a 24-bar solo over an A7 vamp that mixes minor pentatonic with the major third of the chord, using rakes and double stops, without losing the groove.

lessons.title: What's Under Marty Schwartz's Hat? (John Mayer Who Did You Think I Was Guitar Lesson + Tutorial)
How To Play Who Did You Think I Was On Guitar | John Mayer Guitar Lesson + Tutorial + TABS

steps.title: Waiting on the World to Change
steps.description:
[What it is]
The whole song: D, Bm, G and A, with Em7 and G6 alongside them.
The D/F sharp inversion with hammer-ons over the thumb. A sixteenth-note soul comp in the Curtis Mayfield manner. Fills placed between the vocal lines. Then the solo, with its slides.

[Why it matters]
Here his rhythm playing is the whole arrangement. The inversion held with the thumb, the fills between the lines, and the sixteenth-note comp from phase two, all on one record.
If the comp grooves and the fills stay out of the vocal, the rhythm half of this roadmap is finished.

[How to practice]
Verse and chorus from the Andy Guitar lesson. Then the Jorge Aguilera lesson for the way he actually plays it: the inversion, the hammer-ons and the fills.
The solo from the GuitarLessons365 part two.
Play it with the record. Then with a drum loop only. Then under a singer, or under the isolated vocal track.
steps.successCriteria: You can play Waiting on the World to Change with the record from start to finish, comping with the inversion, hammer-ons and fills without covering the vocal, and play the solo at tempo, in one recording.

lessons.title: John Mayer - Waiting On The World To Change guitar lesson tutorial + SOLO
John Mayer - Waiting on the World to Change - Guitar Lesson the way John plays it
Waiting On The World To Change Guitar Lesson Pt.2 - John Mayer - Solo & Outro

steps.title: Your own solo
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two solos of your own, not transcriptions. One over a slow 6/8 ballad in G, one over a medium soul progression in D. Those are the two settings his playing lives in.
You judge them against a checklist of nine things from this roadmap: major and minor mixed, target thirds, space, one laid-back phrase, a motif that comes back, bends in tune, a sixths fill, a rake, and dynamics that peak late.

[Why it matters]
Copying his solos proves you can hear. This proves you can speak.
His own advice is about using vocabulary freely, not reciting licks.
The checklist is there so that freedom stays honest. It is easy to call a solo personal when it is really just the two licks you can already play.

[How to practice]
Improv Prompts — Medium, to get used to playing under a restriction.
Then record 24 bars over the G ballad and 24 over the D progression.
Listen back with the checklist in front of you and re-record until at least seven of the nine items are there without being forced in.
Use the Guitar Lick Dojo licks in G as raw material, but change every one of them before you keep it.
steps.successCriteria: You have two recorded 24-bar solos, one over the G ballad in 6/8 and one over the D progression, in which someone holding the nine-item checklist can tick at least seven in each. You can say where each one happens.

lessons.title: 10 John Mayer Licks in G Major - John Mayer Guitar Licks Lesson with Tabs

steps.title: Play in a trio
steps.description:
[What it is]
Guitar, bass and drums, with no second guitar and no keys.
That means a rhythm part that leaves room for the other two, a comp that stays under a singer, solo sections that grow out of the comp and go back into it, and recovering from a mistake without stopping.
Do it with real players, or with a bass-and-drums play-along.

[Why it matters]
Mayer says of playing with Dead & Company that "there is no lead guitar", and that soloing there like a traditional lead player "sounds terrible". He also says that music taught him how to make a mistake and recover quickly, because it is always pushing ahead.
The Trio records are the model: one guitar carrying rhythm and lead in turn.

[How to practice]
Timing — Switch Subdivisions, so the pocket holds when the part gets busier or thinner.
Then play a 12-bar in A in trio form, with two other players or a play-along: two choruses of comping with stops, two of soloing, then back to comping, calling each change out loud.
Make one deliberate mistake per run and carry on without stopping.
Record five minutes and listen for whether you can still hear the bass and drums underneath you.
steps.successCriteria: A five-minute recorded trio or play-along of a 12-bar in A has clear comping and solo sections, stops that land together, no train wreck, and one deliberate mistake you recover from without stopping.

lessons.title: John Mayer Trio - Who did you think I was - Guitar Lesson (full song)

steps.title: Final: record a three-song set
steps.description:
[What it is]
Three songs, one from each side of his playing, played back to back in one take.
With the tone changes between them, one solo section of your own inside the lead piece, a count-in at the start and a real ending.
Recorded with backing tracks or with other musicians.

[Why it matters]
This is the roadmap's promise made checkable. Everything from the Vaughan cassette to the thumb slap, the equator, the thumb chords and the rig, in one recording you could send to a band.

[How to practice]
Pick one song per side: an acoustic groove piece (Neon or Stop This Train), a thumb-chord rhythm piece (Slow Dancing or Waiting on the World to Change), and a lead piece (Gravity or the Trio song).
Write a one-page plan: the order, the tone setting for each song, where your own solo goes, and how each song starts and ends.
Rehearse the changeovers, not just the songs. Switching hands, touch and tone between an acoustic slap groove and a boosted blues lead is its own skill, and it is where a set falls apart.
Then play all three back to back in every session until the weakest of them stops being obvious. Then record the take.

[What you can do now]
You play thumb-fretted chords with sus4, 6 and 9 decorations, moving bass lines and soul comping.
You play the thumb-slap acoustic groove behind Neon and Stop This Train.
You play blues lead with bends and vibrato in tune, major and minor pentatonic mixed, rakes, sixths, space and a motif that comes back.
You can dial his tone on any clean amp, and you can carry a trio as the only guitarist in it.
steps.successCriteria: You have a one-take recording of three Mayer songs, one per side, played back to back at the records' tempos with backing tracks or musicians, with a count-in, working tone changes, a solo section of your own, and no stops.
